```{=html}
    <section id="rationale" class="case-section">
      <p class="eyebrow"><span class="num">02</span> RESEARCH RATIONALE</p>
      <h2>Why study the changing boundaries between data roles?</h2>

      <div class="rationale-box">
        <p>
          Data analyst work is increasingly moving beyond dashboards and traditional reporting toward deeper business context, automation, and responsibilities that overlap with data science, data engineering, and machine learning. At the same time, AI can automate many routine technical tasks, making the skill of being able to interpret data within a meaningful business context and translate analysis into decisions even more important.
        </p>

        <p>
          Three trends made this especially relevant in 2024: growing demand for AI and advanced analytics, increased emphasis on hybrid skill sets that combine tools such as Python and SQL with business communication, and clearer separation between traditional analytics positions and more specialized AI-focused roles. Remote and hybrid work have also expanded access to opportunities while increasing competition.
        </p>

        <p>
          I expected the market to reward both technical depth and business understanding, with noticeable differences in skills, experience, and compensation between traditional analytics and AI-oriented roles.
        </p>
      </div>
    </section>


    <section id="skills" class="case-section">
      <p class="eyebrow"><span class="num">03</span> SKILLS BY ROLE</p>
      <h2>Which skills are employers looking for?</h2>
      <p class="wide-copy">
        Skill variables were processed independently to preserve the differences between software, specialized, common, and certification skill requirements. I cleaned the raw list fields, exploded them into individual observations, and ranked the most frequently occurring skills within each role category.
      </p>

      <div class="analysis-block">
        <div class="analysis-heading">
          <div>
            <h2>Cleaning and extracting skills</h2>
            <p>The code below is copied directly from my project notebook.</p>
          </div>
          <span class="language-pill">PySpark</span>
        </div>

        <div class="code-card">
          <div class="code-toolbar">
            <div class="window-dots"><b></b><b></b><b></b></div>
            <button class="copy-code">Copy</button>
          </div>
          <pre><code class="language-python"># clean and extract skills
from pyspark.sql.functions import regexp_replace, split, explode, trim, lower, col, lit

# clean the string and remove unwanted characters such as list brackets, quotes, and new lines
def extract_skills(dataframe, skill_col, skill_type):
    cleaned = dataframe.withColumn(
        "SKILL_CLEAN",
        regexp_replace(col(skill_col), r'[\[\]\n"]', "")
    )

# explode so its one row per skill and rename column
    exploded = cleaned.select(
        "ROLE_CATEGORY",
        explode(split(col("SKILL_CLEAN"), ",")).alias("SKILL")
    )

# clean formatting so everything is lower, trim any spaces, and remove empty values
    return exploded.withColumn(
        "SKILL",
        trim(lower(col("SKILL")))
    ).filter(
        (col("SKILL").isNotNull()) &amp; (col("SKILL") != "")
    ).withColumn(
        "SKILL_TYPE",
        lit(skill_type)
    )</code></pre>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="analysis-block">
        <div class="analysis-heading">
          <div>
            <h2>Ranking the top skills by role</h2>
            <p>I used a PySpark window function to identify the top 15 skills inside each role category.</p>
          </div>
          <span class="language-pill">PySpark</span>
        </div>

        <div class="code-card">
          <div class="code-toolbar">
            <div class="window-dots"><b></b><b></b><b></b></div>
            <button class="copy-code">Copy</button>
          </div>
          <pre><code class="language-python"># window function to extract and aggregate skill datasets to identify the top 15 most frequently occurring skills within each role category
from pyspark.sql.window import Window
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, row_number

def get_top_skills_by_role(df):
    counts = df.groupBy("ROLE_CATEGORY", "SKILL").count()

    window = Window.partitionBy("ROLE_CATEGORY").orderBy(col("count").desc())

    ranked = counts.withColumn(
        "rank",
        row_number().over(window)
    ).filter(col("rank") &lt;= 15)

    return ranked</code></pre>
        </div>
      </div>
<br>
```

```{python}
#| echo: false

import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

PORTFOLIO_FONT = "Inter, Helvetica Neue, Arial, sans-serif"
TEXT = "#223047"
MUTED = "#718096"
GRID = "#F1F3F6"

ROLE_COLORS = {
    "Data Analyst": "#7FB3E6",
    "Data Scientist": "#A98BE3",
    "AI Engineer/Analyst": "#6BCB9A"
}

def apply_portfolio_style(fig, height=None):
    fig.update_layout(
        template="plotly_white",
        paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
        plot_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
        font=dict(family=PORTFOLIO_FONT, color=TEXT, size=12),
        title_font=dict(family=PORTFOLIO_FONT, color=TEXT, size=18),
        margin=dict(l=24, r=45, t=76, b=52),
        hoverlabel=dict(
            bgcolor="white",
            bordercolor="#E4E7EC",
            font=dict(family=PORTFOLIO_FONT, color=TEXT)
        )
    )
    if height:
        fig.update_layout(height=height)

    fig.update_xaxes(
        showgrid=True,
        gridcolor=GRID,
        zeroline=False,
        tickfont=dict(family=PORTFOLIO_FONT, color=MUTED, size=11),
        title_font=dict(family=PORTFOLIO_FONT, color=MUTED, size=12),
        automargin=True
    )
    fig.update_yaxes(
        showgrid=False,
        zeroline=False,
        tickfont=dict(family=PORTFOLIO_FONT, color=TEXT, size=11),
        automargin=True
    )
    return fig

def role_skill_figure(data, title, top_n=15):
    roles = ["Data Analyst", "Data Scientist", "AI Engineer/Analyst"]

    fig = make_subplots(
        rows=3,
        cols=1,
        subplot_titles=roles,
        vertical_spacing=0.075
    )

    for row_num, role in enumerate(roles, start=1):
        rows = sorted(data[role], key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:top_n]
        rows = rows[::-1]

        fig.add_trace(
            go.Bar(
                x=[v for _, v in rows],
                y=[k for k, _ in rows],
                orientation="h",
                text=[f"{v:,}" for _, v in rows],
                textposition="outside",
                cliponaxis=False,
                marker=dict(
                    color=ROLE_COLORS[role],
                    line=dict(width=0)
                ),
                hovertemplate="<b>%{y}</b><br>%{x:,} postings<extra></extra>",
                showlegend=False
            ),
            row=row_num,
            col=1
        )

        fig.update_xaxes(
            title_text="Number of job postings",
            row=row_num,
            col=1
        )

    apply_portfolio_style(fig, height=1220)
    fig.update_layout(
        title=dict(
            text=title,
            x=0.01,
            xanchor="left"
        ),
        bargap=0.28
    )

    # Make the three role headings match their bar colors.
    for annotation, role in zip(fig.layout.annotations, roles):
        annotation.update(
            font=dict(
                family=PORTFOLIO_FONT,
                size=15,
                color=ROLE_COLORS[role]
            ),
            x=0,
            xanchor="left"
        )

    return fig
```

```{=html}
    <section id="clustering" class="case-section ml-section">
  <p class="eyebrow"><span class="num">05</span> UNSUPERVISED LEARNING</p>

  <div class="ml-intro">
    <div>
      <h2>Can job postings reveal natural career groupings without relying on job titles?</h2>

      <p class="wide-copy">
        Job titles are not always consistent across employers. I used K-Means clustering
        to explore whether data-related job postings would naturally form groups based
        on their underlying characteristics rather than their predefined role labels.
      </p>

      <p class="wide-copy">
        K-Means is an unsupervised learning algorithm, so the model was not given a
        target variable to predict. Instead, it searched for similarity across salary,
        minimum experience, education, and feature engineered technical-skill indicators.
      </p>
    </div>

    <div class="ml-method-card">
      <span class="method-label">MODEL</span>
      <strong>K-Means</strong>
      <p>Unsupervised clustering</p>
      <div class="method-tags">
        <span>PySpark ML</span>
        <span>k = 4</span>
        <span>PCA</span>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>


  <div class="ml-subsection">
    <p class="mini-eyebrow">MODEL PIPELINE</p>
    <h3>From job postings to interpretable clusters</h3>

    <div class="ml-pipeline">
      <div class="pipeline-step">
        <div class="pipeline-icon"><i class="bi bi-funnel"></i></div>
        <span>01</span>
        <strong>Filter</strong>
        <p>Focus on relevant data roles</p>
      </div>

      <div class="pipeline-arrow">→</div>

      <div class="pipeline-step">
        <div class="pipeline-icon"><i class="bi bi-sliders"></i></div>
        <span>02</span>
        <strong>Engineer</strong>
        <p>Create binary skill indicators</p>
      </div>

      <div class="pipeline-arrow">→</div>

      <div class="pipeline-step">
        <div class="pipeline-icon"><i class="bi bi-bar-chart"></i></div>
        <span>03</span>
        <strong>Scale</strong>
        <p>Standardize model features</p>
      </div>

      <div class="pipeline-arrow">→</div>

      <div class="pipeline-step">
        <div class="pipeline-icon"><i class="bi bi-graph-up"></i></div>
        <span>04</span>
        <strong>Select k</strong>
        <p>Compare WSSSE solutions</p>
      </div>

      <div class="pipeline-arrow">→</div>

      <div class="pipeline-step">
        <div class="pipeline-icon"><i class="bi bi-diagram-3"></i></div>
        <span>05</span>
        <strong>Cluster</strong>
        <p>Fit the K-Means model</p>
      </div>

      <div class="pipeline-arrow">→</div>

      <div class="pipeline-step">
        <div class="pipeline-icon"><i class="bi bi-search"></i></div>
        <span>06</span>
        <strong>Interpret</strong>
        <p>PCA + cluster profiles</p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="ml-subsection">
    <p class="mini-eyebrow">01 — FEATURE ENGINEERING</p>
    <h3>How can job postings be represented by their technical skills?</h3>

    <p class="wide-copy">
     I first combined the available skill fields into a single text representation. I then converted the presence of selected technical skills into binary features (1 = present, 0 = absent), allowing each job posting’s skill profile to be represented numerically for clustering.
    </p>

    <div class="feature-chips">
      <span><i class="bi bi-currency-dollar"></i> Salary</span>
      <span><i class="bi bi-briefcase"></i> Experience</span>
      <span><i class="bi bi-mortarboard"></i> Education</span>
      <span><i class="bi bi-code-slash"></i> Technical Skills</span>
    </div>

    <div class="ml-code-group">
      <div class="code-card">
        <div class="code-toolbar">
          <div class="window-dots"><b></b><b></b><b></b></div>
          <span class="language-pill">PySpark</span>
        </div>
        <pre><code class="language-python"># combine all skill text
from pyspark.sql.functions import concat_ws, coalesce, lit

skill_cols = [
    "SKILLS_NAME",
    "SPECIALIZED_SKILLS_NAME",
    "SOFTWARE_SKILLS_NAME",
    "COMMON_SKILLS_NAME"
]

df_roles = df_roles.withColumn(
    "ALL_SKILLS_TEXT",
    lower(
        concat_ws(
            " ",
            *[coalesce(col(c), lit("")) for c in skill_cols]
        )
    )
)</code></pre>
      </div>

      <div class="code-card">
        <div class="code-toolbar">
          <div class="window-dots"><b></b><b></b><b></b></div>
          <span class="language-pill">PySpark</span>
        </div>
        <pre><code class="language-python"># create binary skill features
from pyspark.sql.functions import regexp_extract

technical_skills = [
    "python","sql","excel","tableau","power bi",
    "machine learning","artificial intelligence",
    "data analysis","statistics","math",
    "linear algebra","probability","data visualization",
    "spark","aws","computer science"
]

df_skill_features = df_roles

for skill in technical_skills:
    clean_name = skill.replace(" ", "_").replace("-", "_").replace("/", "_")
    pattern = rf"\\b{skill.lower()}\\b"
    
    df_skill_features = df_skill_features.withColumn(
        f"skill_{clean_name}",
        (regexp_extract(col("ALL_SKILLS_TEXT"), pattern, 0) != "").cast("int")
    )</code></pre>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>


  <div class="ml-subsection">
    <p class="mini-eyebrow">02 — PREPARING FEATURES FOR CLUSTERING</p>
    <h3>Preparing the skill profiles for K-Means</h3>

    <p class="wide-copy">
      After creating the binary skill indicators, I combined salary, minimum experience,
      education level, and the engineered skill variables into a single feature vector.
      PySpark's K-Means implementation expects the model inputs in this vector format.
      I then standardized the vector before applying the distance-based clustering model.
    </p>
    
    <div class="ml-callout">
      <div class="callout-icon"><i class="bi bi-rulers"></i></div>
      <div>
        <strong>Why standardize?</strong>
        <p>
          K-Means groups observations using distance. Salary, experience, education,
          and binary skill indicators are measured on different numerical scales, so
          standardization keeps a high-magnitude variable such as salary from dominating
          the distance calculation simply because of its units.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>


  <div class="ml-subsection">
    <p class="mini-eyebrow">03 — CHOOSING THE NUMBER OF CLUSTERS</p>
    <h3>How many groups best represent the job market?</h3>

    <p class="wide-copy">
      I trained candidate K-Means models for k = 2, 3, and 4 and compared their
      within-cluster sum of squared errors (WSSSE). Lower WSSSE means observations
      sit closer to their assigned cluster centers. The error continued to decline
      across the tested values, but the curve did not show a sharp elbow.
    </p>

    <div class="ml-result-layout">
      <div class="code-card">
        <div class="code-toolbar">
          <div class="window-dots"><b></b><b></b><b></b></div>
          <span class="language-pill">PySpark ML</span>
        </div>
        <pre><code class="language-python"># compare candidate values of k
cost = []
k_values = range(2, 5)

for k in k_values:
    kmeans = KMeans(
        k=k,
        featuresCol="scaled_features",
        seed=42
    )
    model = kmeans.fit(df_model)
    cost.append(model.summary.trainingCost)</code></pre>
      </div>

      <figure class="ml-process-figure">
        <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Elbow plot comparing WSSSE for two, three, and four K-Means clusters." />
        <figcaption><strong>Elbow-method comparison.</strong> WSSSE falls from k = 2 through k = 4 without a dramatic bend, so the plot does not identify one unambiguous cluster count.</figcaption>
      </figure>
    </div>

    <div class="ml-decision">
      <div class="decision-number">4</div>
      <div>
        <span>SELECTED CLUSTER COUNT</span>
        <h3>Why k = 4?</h3>
        <p>
          I selected four clusters as an exploratory balance between additional
          segmentation and interpretability. Because the tested WSSSE curve does not
          contain a dramatic elbow, I do not treat four as the single “true” number
          of occupational groups; instead, I use it as a useful structure for examining
          different skill and job profiles.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>


  <div class="ml-subsection">
    <p class="mini-eyebrow">04 — K-MEANS CLUSTERING</p>

    <div class="analysis-heading">
      <div>
        <h3>Grouping postings by technical skill profile</h3>
        <p>Using the selected k = 4, I fit the final model on the standardized feature vectors and assigned each posting to its nearest cluster centroid.</p>
      </div>
      <span class="language-pill">PySpark ML</span>
    </div>

    <div class="code-card">
      <div class="code-toolbar">
        <div class="window-dots"><b></b><b></b><b></b></div>
      </div>
      <pre><code class="language-python"># fit the selected four-cluster solution
kmeans = KMeans(k=4, featuresCol="scaled_features", seed=42)
model = kmeans.fit(df_model)
df_clustered = model.transform(df_model)</code></pre>
    </div>
  </div>


  <div class="ml-subsection">
    <p class="mini-eyebrow">05 — INTERPRETING THE CLUSTERS</p>
    <h3>What makes each cluster different?</h3>

    <p class="wide-copy">
      I profiled each cluster by examining its dominant skills and broader job
      characteristics. The resulting groups were interpretable, but they represented
      different levels and types of specialization rather than four perfectly isolated
      occupations.
    </p>

    <div class="cluster-profile-grid">
      <div class="cluster-profile">
        <div class="cluster-number">C0</div>
        <div>
          <span>PROFILE</span>
          <h3>Traditional Analytics</h3>
          <p>SQL-heavy analytical work with less emphasis on advanced ML and statistical skills.</p>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="cluster-profile">
        <div class="cluster-number">C1</div>
        <div>
          <span>PROFILE</span>
          <h3>Data Science</h3>
          <p>Greater emphasis on machine learning, statistics, probability, and quantitative depth.</p>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="cluster-profile">
        <div class="cluster-number">C2</div>
        <div>
          <span>PROFILE</span>
          <h3>Generalist / Mixed</h3>
          <p>A more heterogeneous group with weaker concentration around one technical specialty.</p>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="cluster-profile">
        <div class="cluster-number">C3</div>
        <div>
          <span>PROFILE</span>
          <h3>Business Intelligence</h3>
          <p>Strong SQL combined with BI, dashboarding, and visualization-oriented tools.</p>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <figure class="ml-process-figure">
      <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Heatmap of average skill presence across four K-Means clusters." />
      
    </figure>

    <div class="figure-observations">
      <div><strong>Cluster 1</strong><p>Shows the broadest technical profile, with strong SQL, data analysis, Tableau, Power BI, Python, visualization, and statistics presence.</p></div>
      <div><strong>Cluster 3</strong><p>Is strongly anchored by SQL and data analysis, but has much lower presence of the broader BI and advanced technical skills.</p></div>
      <div><strong>Across clusters</strong><p>The groups differ mainly in skill combinations and intensity rather than completely exclusive skill sets.</p></div>
    </div>
  </div>


  <div class="ml-subsection">
    <p class="mini-eyebrow">06 — PCA VISUALIZATION</p>
    <h3>How distinct are the clusters in a lower-dimensional view?</h3>

    <p class="wide-copy">
      I used Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to project the high-dimensional
      model features into two dimensions. This makes the cluster structure easier
      to inspect visually, although PCA necessarily compresses information from the
      original feature space.
    </p>

    <div class="ml-result-layout">
      

      <figure class="ml-process-figure">
        <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="PCA scatter plot showing substantial overlap among the four K-Means clusters." />
        <figcaption><strong>PCA view of the four-cluster solution.</strong> The colors overlap substantially rather than forming four isolated clouds, reinforcing that the underlying job profiles share many characteristics.</figcaption>
      </figure>
    </div>

    <div class="insight-banner ml-main-finding">
      <span class="finding-kicker">KEY MODEL FINDING</span>
      <strong>Data careers appear to exist on a spectrum.</strong>
      <p>
        The elbow curve, cluster skill profiles, and PCA view tell a consistent story:
        meaningful differences in skill composition exist, but the boundaries are not
        rigid. Traditional analytics, BI, data science, and AI-oriented postings share
        many underlying capabilities and differ more by combinations and depth of skills
        than by completely separate occupational categories.
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>


  <div class="ml-subsection">
    <p class="mini-eyebrow">06 — CONCLUSION </p>
    <h3>MODEL LIMITATIONS &amp; NEXT TESTS</h3>

    <div class="limitation-card">
      <i class="bi bi-info-circle"></i>
      <div>
        <h3>Clustering is exploratory, not ground truth.</h3>
        <p>
          K-Means assumes distance-based, relatively compact clusters. The gradual
          WSSSE curve and PCA overlap indicate that this labor-market data does not
          naturally divide into sharply separated groups. PCA also compresses the
          full feature space into two dimensions, so some structure can be lost in
          visualization.
        </p>
        <p>
          If I extended the model, I would test a wider range of k values using
          silhouette scores, compare cluster membership against the original role
          categories, and evaluate cluster stability across several random seeds.
          Those checks would help determine whether the observed groupings are
          consistently reproducible or primarily exploratory.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

</section>

    <section id="literature" class="case-section">
      <p class="eyebrow"><span class="num">06</span> LITERATURE REVIEW</p>
      <h2>Do the findings align with other labor-market research?</h2>

      <div class="literature-box">
        <h3>Skills-based hiring &amp; hybrid skill sets</h3>

        <p>
          Kobets et al. (2024) analyzed 3,744 job postings and used K-means clustering to identify four data-role groupings: Data Analyst &amp; Engineer, Data Platform Engineer, Data Science &amp; Engineering Specialist, and Cloud Data Engineer. Their results similarly suggest that modern data roles are increasingly defined by combinations of competencies rather than job titles alone.
        </p>

        <p>
          The study highlights Python, SQL, cloud platforms such as AWS and Azure, data engineering, analytics, and machine learning as recurring requirements. It also identifies a gap between academic training and industry needs, reinforcing the importance of continuous upskilling and hybrid technical/business skill sets.
        </p>

        <p>
          This provides useful external support for the patterns in my own analysis: SQL and Python function as core skills, specialized tools distinguish different career paths, and skill composition often provides a clearer picture of role structure than title alone.
        </p>

        <p class="source-note">
          Reference:
          <a href="https://aait.od.ua/index.php/journal/article/view/154/154">
            Kobets, Gulin, and Nosov (2024)
          </a>
        </p>
      </div>
    </section>

  </main>
</div>

<script>
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () {
  const navLinks = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll("#case-scroll-nav a"));
  const sections = navLinks
    .map(link => document.querySelector(link.getAttribute("href")))
    .filter(Boolean);

  function setActive(id) {
    navLinks.forEach(link => {
      const active = link.getAttribute("href") === "#" + id;
      link.classList.toggle("active", active);
    });
  }

  navLinks.forEach(link => {
    link.addEventListener("click", function (e) {
      const target = document.querySelector(this.getAttribute("href"));
      if (!target) return;
      e.preventDefault();
      target.scrollIntoView({ behavior: "smooth", block: "start" });
      setActive(target.id);
    });
  });

  const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
    entries => {
      const visible = entries
        .filter(entry => entry.isIntersecting)
        .sort((a, b) => b.intersectionRatio - a.intersectionRatio);

      if (visible.length) setActive(visible[0].target.id);
    },
    {
      root: null,
      rootMargin: "-18% 0px -60% 0px",
      threshold: [0.05, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5]
    }
  );

  sections.forEach(section => observer.observe(section));

  window.addEventListener("scroll", function () {
    if (window.innerHeight + window.scrollY >= document.body.offsetHeight - 8) {
      setActive(sections[sections.length - 1].id);
    }
  });
});
</script>
```
